issues.legal_issue: A High Court may require an application for certification of an intra-court appeal to be made orally and immediately after judgment, where the requirement regulates rather than removes the right of appeal.
material_facts: A High Court rule required a party seeking certification for a further appeal to apply orally and immediately after the appellate judgment was delivered.
The appellant sought certification later by letter and subsequent oral application, which the judge refused as untimely.
issues.conclusion: The rule was valid because it regulated the manner and timing of the application without taking away the right conferred by the Letters Patent.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 15 of the Letters Patent provided for an appeal where the judge declared the case fit for appeal, and Clause 37 empowered the High Court to regulate civil proceedings. The court relied on Union of India v. Ram Kanwar, which upheld the High Court’s power to prescribe procedural requirements for an appeal.

predicates.intra_court_certificate_process: A party seeks certification for a further appeal after a single judge has decided an appeal from an appellate decree or order.
predicates.rule_sets_application_timing: The court rule prescribes when and how the party must request certification.
predicates.rule_preserves_appeal_right: The rule regulates the request for certification without removing the right of appeal.

issues.definition: When a court rule sets the timing and manner of requesting certification in an intra-court appeal but preserves the right of appeal, the rule is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to pursue an available intra-court appeal does not impose an inflexible bar on the Supreme Court’s discretionary consideration of a special-leave appeal.
material_facts: The appellant did not request certification for a further High Court appeal immediately after judgment and gave no explanation for that failure.
The Supreme Court granted special leave, and the case proceeded beyond interim orders and preparation of the record before the preliminary objection was considered.
issues.conclusion: The failure to pursue the further High Court appeal did not automatically bar the Supreme Court from hearing the special-leave appeal; whether to exercise its jurisdiction depended on the circumstances of the case.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 confers a wide discretionary jurisdiction, and there is no inflexible rule that special leave must be refused whenever an available Letters Patent appeal was not pursued. The court relied on Penu Balakrishna Iyer v. Sri Ariva M. Ramaswami Iyer and treated the decision whether to exercise jurisdiction as case-specific.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_second_appellate_decision and further_high_court_appeal_not_pursued and special_leave_granted and case_progressed_beyond_interim_stage

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_second_appella: A party seeks special leave to challenge a High Court decision in a second appeal.
predicates.further_high_court_appeal_not_pursued: The party did not pursue an available further appeal within the prescribed procedure.
predicates.special_leave_granted: The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal.
predicates.case_progressed_beyond_interim_stage: The case proceeded beyond interim orders and preparation of the record before the objection to its competence was considered.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal from a second appellate decision has been granted and has progressed beyond the interim stage, failure to pursue a further High Court appeal does not necessarily prevent the Supreme Court from hearing the merits.

issues.legal_issue: A voluntary transfer of disputed immovable property by a party during a pending partition suit is subject to the outcome of the suit when it may affect another litigant’s rights under the decree.
material_facts: A partition suit concerning joint-family properties was pending before the voluntary sale of some of those properties.
The sale was made by the managing family member and some of his sons, did not purport to bind the whole family, and was not shown to have been made on behalf of the family for legal necessity.
The sale was supported by consideration, but the purchaser’s claimed debts and the sale did not establish that the transfer bound the entire family.
issues.conclusion: The voluntary sale was affected by lis pendens and could not prejudice the other family member’s rights under the partition decree.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act applies to transfers or other dealings by a party during a non-collusive suit in which rights to immovable property are directly and specifically in question, where the dealing may affect another party’s rights under the decree. The doctrine preserves the court’s control over the subject matter. The court also relied on K.N. Lal v. Ganeshi Ram to reject the contention that an earlier attachment removed property from the operation of lis pendens, and distinguished Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh as concerning the particular nature of a pre-emption right.

predicates.partition_suit_pending: A partition proceeding is pending in court.
predicates.disputed_immovable_property_at_issue: The transferred immovable property is directly and specifically involved in the proceeding.
predicates.party_voluntarily_transfers_property_dur: A party to the proceeding voluntarily transfers or deals with the property while the proceeding is pending.
predicates.transfer_may_affect_another_litigants_de: The transfer may affect another litigant’s rights under the decree in the proceeding.

issues.definition: A voluntary dealing by a party with disputed property during a pending partition suit remains subject to the decree when it may affect another litigant’s rights.

issues.legal_issue: A revenue sale to recover a statutory loan cannot, merely because the dues are recoverable as land revenue, displace other family members’ interests beyond the borrower’s interest and any land legally charged for the loan.
material_facts: During a pending partition suit, property included in the suit was sold at a revenue auction to recover a loan granted to one family member under a land-improvement loan statute.
The borrower claimed that he had taken the loan individually to purchase a pumping set, and the evidence did not establish that he had borrowed on behalf of the joint family.
The statutory recovery provisions allowed recovery from the borrower and, for land benefiting from the loan, from that land; they also protected certain prior interests.
The sale certificate did not establish that every property sold had benefited from the loan, and the lower courts directed that the relevant properties be identified.
issues.conclusion: The statutory recovery did not give a general priority allowing sale of property beyond the borrower’s interest. The sale could be effective against land for whose improvement the loan was taken, while the remaining disputed property remained subject to lis pendens; the matter required identification of the land benefiting from the loan.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(1)(a) and (c), including its proviso, of the Land Improvement Loans Act limited recovery to the borrower and land benefiting from the loan, while protecting specified pre-existing interests. Section 42 of the Madras Revenue Recovery Act dealt with sales free of encumbrances, but statutory recovery powers were confined to what the statute authorized. The court also relied on Builders Supply Corporation v. Union of India concerning the State’s claimed paramount right, and Attorney General v. de Keyser’s Royal Hotel Ltd. for the proposition that statutory terms govern where recovery is based on statute. The concurrence relied on Samarendra Nath Sinha v. Krishna Kumar Nag and Kedar Nath Lal v. Ganesh Ram in recognizing that lis pendens principles can apply to involuntary sales, while a pre-existing charge may nevertheless be enforced.

rule.if: revenue_sale_during_partition_suit and statutory_loan_for_borrower and family_liability_not_established and (loan_benefited_sold_land or sold_property_exceeds_borrowers_interest)

predicates.revenue_sale_during_partition_suit: A revenue authority sells property involved in a pending partition proceeding.
predicates.statutory_loan_for_borrower: The sale is to recover a statutory loan made to a family member as borrower.
predicates.family_liability_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the borrower incurred the loan on behalf of the family.
predicates.loan_benefited_sold_land: The loan was granted for the improvement of the land sold.
predicates.sold_property_exceeds_borrowers_interest: The sale includes property or interests beyond those of the borrower.

issues.definition: When a statutory loan was incurred by a borrower individually during a pending partition proceeding, revenue recovery cannot reach beyond the borrower’s interest and land shown to have benefited from and been charged for the loan.
